options.text: The data could be normally distributed, because it is roughly symmetrical with a single central peak.
The data cannot be normally distributed, because the two sides are not exactly equal.
options.why: Treats 'normally distributed' as requiring perfect symmetry, when real data only needs to be approximately symmetrical.

options.text: The data cannot be normally distributed, because it is positively skewed.
options.why: Names a skew that is not there; the columns fall away on both sides rather than trailing off to the right.

options.text: The data cannot be normally distributed, because the frequencies are not all equal.
options.why: Confuses a normal distribution with a uniform (flat) one; a bell curve must not have equal frequencies.

questions.solution_text:
The tallest column is at $8$, near the middle of the display.
The frequencies fall away on both sides, $10$, $4$, $1$ to the left and $11$, $5$, $1$ to the right.
The display is approximately symmetrical with a single central peak, so the data could be normally distributed.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the number of emails received by an office on each of $49$ days.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} \text{Emails} & 50 & 51 & 52 & 53 & 54 & 55 & 56 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 2 & 7 & 19 & 11 & 6 & 3 & 1 \end{array}$
Which statement about this data is correct?

options.text: It is not normal, because the peak is left of centre with a long tail stretching to the right.
It is normal, because the frequencies rise to a peak and then fall away.
options.why: Checks only for a peak and ignores symmetry; a positively skewed display also rises then falls.

options.text: It is not normal, because it has two peaks.
options.why: Misreads the table as bimodal; there is a single largest frequency of $19$.

options.text: It is normal, because there are seven different values and the frequencies add to an odd number.
options.why: Uses the number of classes and the total frequency, neither of which has anything to do with shape.

questions.solution_text:
The largest frequency is $19$ at the value $52$, which is the third of seven columns.
On the left the frequencies fall from $19$ to $7$ then $2$, but on the right they fall from $11$ to $6$, $3$, $1$, so the right-hand tail is longer.
The display is positively skewed rather than symmetrical, so it is not normally distributed.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the times, to the nearest hour, that $32$ people spent on a task.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Hours} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 12 & 4 & 2 & 3 & 11 \end{array}$
Which statement best explains why this data is not normally distributed?

options.text: The display has two peaks, one at each end, with a dip in the middle instead of a single central peak.
The display is symmetrical, and a normal distribution must be asymmetrical.
options.why: Reverses the definition; a normal distribution is symmetrical, and symmetry alone is not what rules this display out.

options.text: The mean of the data is not zero, and a normal distribution must have a mean of zero.
options.why: Confuses a normal distribution with the standardised z-scores, whose mean is $0$.

options.text: The frequencies do not add to $100$, so they cannot form a normal distribution.
options.why: Confuses frequencies with percentages; the total frequency has no bearing on the shape.

questions.solution_text:
The two tallest columns are at $1$ hour and at $5$ hours, and the smallest frequency is in the middle at $3$ hours.
The display is bimodal, with a dip where a bell curve has its peak.
So the data is not normally distributed.

options.why: Reads the tallest curve as the most spread out; a tall narrow curve has the smallest standard deviation.
Chooses the middle curve, treating standard deviation as a middling or average property rather than reading the width.

options.text: All three have the same standard deviation.
options.why: Assumes curves on one axis must share a spread; the curves clearly differ in width.

questions.solution_text:
The standard deviation measures spread, so the more spread out a normal curve is, the wider and flatter it looks.
Curve $Z$ is the widest and lowest of the three, and curve $X$ is the narrowest and tallest.
Curve $Z$ has the largest standard deviation.

questions.question_text: One of these variables is measured for a very large group. Which is most likely to be approximately normally distributed?

options.text: The masses of $2000$ newborn babies born in one year
The number of car accidents each driver had last year
options.why: Almost every driver records $0$, giving one huge column at the left and a long right tail — strongly positively skewed.

options.text: The winning numbers drawn in $2000$ lottery draws
options.why: Every number is equally likely, so the display is flat (uniform) with no central peak.

options.text: The number of days in each month of the last $150$ years
options.why: Only the values $28$ to $31$ occur, and $31$ is by far the most common, so the display is a few unequal columns, not a bell.

questions.solution_text:
Birth masses cluster around a middle value, with fewer babies as you move away from it in either direction, and roughly as many above the middle as below.
That is a symmetrical, single-peaked, bell-shaped display.
The masses of the newborn babies are most likely to be approximately normally distributed.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the scores of $60$ students on a test.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{Score} & 10 & 11 & 12 & 13 & 14 \\ \hline \text{Frequency} & 5 & 12 & 26 & 12 & 5 \end{array}$
Which statement about this data is correct?

options.text: The mean, median and mode are all $12$, and the display is symmetrical with a single central peak, so the data could be normally distributed.
The mean is $12$ but the mode is $26$, so the averages are not equal and the data is not normal.
options.why: Quotes the largest frequency as the mode instead of the score that has that frequency.

options.text: The mean, median and mode are all $12$, so the data must be normally distributed whatever its shape.
options.why: Treats equal averages as sufficient; a skewed or spiked display can also have equal averages, so the shape must be checked too.

options.text: The median is $30$, since $60$ scores means the middle is at $30$, so the averages are not equal.
options.why: Reports the position of the middle value rather than the score sitting in that position.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Mean} = \dfrac{10(5)+11(12)+12(26)+13(12)+14(5)}{60}$
$= \dfrac{720}{60}$
$= 12$
The running totals are $5$, $17$, $43$, so the $30$th and $31$st scores are both $12$ and the median is $12$.
The largest frequency is $26$, so the mode is $12$.
The frequencies $5$, $12$, $26$, $12$, $5$ are symmetrical about a single central peak, so the data could be normally distributed.

options.text: The data is not normally distributed, because the peak is near the right-hand end with a long tail stretching to the left.
The data is normally distributed, because most of the scores are close together.
options.why: Uses closeness of the scores instead of shape; a skewed display can also be tightly bunched.

options.text: The data is not normally distributed, because there is no column at a score of $4$ or below.
options.why: Treats missing low scores as the fault; a bell curve is also limited to the values that actually occur.

options.text: The data is normally distributed, because there is exactly one tallest column.
options.why: Checks only for a single peak and skips the symmetry test, which is what this display fails.

questions.solution_text:
The tallest column is at a score of $9$, which is the fifth of six columns.
On the left the frequencies fall away through $11$, $5$, $2$, $1$, but on the right there is only the single column of $14$.
The tail stretches to the left, so the display is negatively skewed rather than symmetrical, and the data is not normally distributed.

options.text: $H$ has the larger mean, and the two curves have the same standard deviation.
$G$ has the larger mean, and the two curves have the same standard deviation.
options.why: Reads the horizontal axis backwards; the mean sits under the peak, and $H$'s peak is further right.

options.text: $H$ has the larger mean and also the larger standard deviation.
options.why: Assumes a curve further to the right must also be more spread out; the two curves are the same width.

options.text: The two curves have the same mean but different standard deviations.
options.why: Swaps the two features: it is the means that differ here and the widths that match.

questions.solution_text:
A normal curve is symmetrical about its mean, so each mean sits under its own peak.
The peak of $H$ is further to the right than the peak of $G$, so $H$ has the larger mean.
The two curves are the same height and the same width, so they have the same standard deviation.
